The exercise wording attributed to Shakespeare is separate from the narrator\'s teaching voice.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The voice in one original passage\\r\\n\\r\\nThe following is a new calibration passage. Its example was created for this guide; it is not a source quotation or an approved bootcamp page.\\r\\n\\r\\n> A conditional tells us that if one thing is true, something else has to be true too.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Suppose a shop has this rule: **Every parcel with a blue sticker has been inspected.**\\r\\n>\\r\\n> You pick up a parcel with a blue sticker. What do you know about it?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> It has been inspected. The rule covers every parcel with that sticker, including the one in your hand. A blue-sticker parcel that hadn\'t been inspected would break the rule.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Now turn the parcel over. It has an inspection stamp, but you can\'t see a blue sticker. Does it have to have one?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We don\'t know. The rule tells us something about parcels with blue stickers. It doesn\'t tell us that every inspected parcel gets a sticker.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> That\'s the distinction we need: **what the sentence makes certain, and what it leaves open.**\\r\\n\\r\\nNotice the opening definition before the example, the small prediction, the explanation connecting the rule to the case, and the change in what the reader is given. The last sentence names a distinction the reader has just seen. The passage has a conversational rhythm because it follows a person\'s thoughts. Casual vocabulary alone would not accomplish that.\\r\\n\\r\\nIn an interactive lesson, pause after the first question and again after the inspection-stamp question. Reveal each explanation after the learner has had an opportunity to answer. The printed passage shows the whole progression for calibration.\\r\\n\\r\\n## How the teacher relates to the reader\\r\\n\\r\\n### The reader is beside the teacher\\r\\n\\r\\nThe narrator talks directly to someone doing the work. “Let\'s,” “you,” and “we” keep the reader involved. The writing seldom steps back to describe what students generally do. It asks this reader to notice, try, decide, or check something now.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe reader is treated as capable of understanding ordinary meaning. The teacher supplies support when a technical step is new. In the opening, the source first gives the literal relationship, then asks the reader to take its certainty seriously. Later, it encourages a guess before revealing the contrapositive. These are expectations of participation, not claims that everything should feel easy.\\r\\n\\r\\n**For our writing:** speak to the reader without making their intelligence the subject. Do not copy a line such as “Because you\'re a thinking human.” Give them a manageable question and the information to answer it. If they miss it, explain the precise move that went wrong.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Confidence lives in the reasoning\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source is decisive about a valid consequence. It also says “We don\'t know” when the information cannot settle a question. These two kinds of confidence belong together. Clear teaching can be certain about the limits of what is known.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe teacher does not apologize for asking the reader to think. The explanation makes the request reasonable. In the FAQ, the narrator acknowledges early mistakes and explains the value of practicing anyway. The tone combines patience with a specific demand: attempt the question, write the diagram, inspect the error.\\r\\n\\r\\n**For our writing:** state the consequence plainly and show why. Preserve legitimate uncertainty. Avoid changing a logical “could” into “must” to make the prose sound stronger. Avoid guarantees about learning outcomes, timing, or score changes unless we have evidence.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Warmth points at the work\\r\\n\\r\\nEncouragement is usually tied to an action. The reader can look back at the lesson, make a provisional attempt, learn from a wrong translation, or build confidence by checking work. The warmth comes from useful help and a teacher who expects progress.\\r\\n\\r\\nUseful form:\\r\\n\\r\\n> If the direction felt unclear, read the statement back in ordinary English. What does it say you need? Keep that complete idea in your diagram.\\r\\n\\r\\nWeak form:\\r\\n\\r\\n> You\'ve got this! Conditionals are easy once you know the trick!\\r\\n\\r\\nThe weak version offers reassurance without a way forward and minimizes the actual difficulty.\\r\\n\\r\\n### “I,” “we,” and “you” have different jobs\\r\\n\\r\\n| Pronoun | What it does in the source | Use in our material |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| **You** | Gives the reader an action or asks for a decision. | “Try the sentence in the other direction. Does it still say the same thing?” |\\r\\n| **We / let\'s** | Makes the explanation a shared investigation. | “Let\'s keep the rule and change the fact.” |\\r\\n| **I**, thinking aloud | Shows the teacher making a decision: noticing an indicator, identifying its target, placing a label. | “I see ‘requires.’ What does it say is required?” |\\r\\n| **I**, hypothetical | Places the speaker inside a condition. | “If I\'m taking this course, what does the sentence say I need?” |\\r\\n| **I**, personal judgment | Gives a recommendation or reports experience. | Use only a genuine Joshua judgment or verified experience. Do not borrow the source narrator\'s student history. |\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep these roles stable. Do not rotate pronouns for cosmetic variety. In a platform instruction, “you” may be enough. In a teacher-authored walkthrough, “I” can make a decision visible. Marketing remains governed by its separate platform voice.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Sentence length and spoken cadence\\r\\n\\r\\n### Short sentences settle; longer sentences explain\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source does not make every sentence short. A longer sentence introduces a situation, explains motivation, or qualifies advice. Short sentences supply a result, mark a limit, or redirect attention.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe opening at HTML line 144 moves from a definition to a plain rephrasing and then the two-word landing “That\'s it.” Later, the source uses several brief sentences to think through a missing requirement, then states the consequence. The broad-purpose paragraph at line 152 is substantially longer. Its job is to explain why understanding the relationship matters across varied wording.\\r\\n\\r\\n**For our writing:** let each sentence carry a manageable thought. A difficult inference may need several sentences. Do not trim away the intermediate reason just to produce a punchy conclusion. A short landing belongs after the explanation has earned it.\\r\\n\\r\\nOriginal rhythm:\\r\\n\\r\\n> The inspection stamp tells us the parcel was inspected. It doesn\'t tell us which sticker the shop gave it afterward. The rule hasn\'t answered that question.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe first sentence identifies what is known. The second identifies the missing connection. The third closes the uncertainty.\\r\\n\\r\\n### The observed numbers are calibration, not quotas\\r\\n\\r\\nAn [approximate prose analysis](../raw/sources/conditional-reasoning-voice-standard/analysis-metrics.json) selects unclassified HTML paragraph elements, excluding the drill and obscured-line marker. It includes prose inside notes and FAQ answers, but excludes displayed examples, table cells, headings, and many short callouts. Words are alphanumeric tokens with internal apostrophes; sentences are split after `.`, `!`, or `?` followed by whitespace. This is a reproducible rough measure, not a linguistic parser.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Measure in that subset | Observation |\\r\\n|---|---:|\\r\\n| Prose paragraphs | 73 |\\r\\n| Prose words | 2,743 |\\r\\n| Approximate sentences | 223 |\\r\\n| Median sentence length | 10 words |\\r\\n| Mean sentence length | 12.3 words |\\r\\n| Sentence range | 1 to 53 words |\\r\\n| Sentences of 8 words or fewer | 76 |\\r\\n| Sentences over 25 words | 15 |\\r\\n| Median paragraph length | 33 words |\\r\\n| Mean paragraph length | 37.6 words |\\r\\n| Paragraph range | 4 to 112 words |\\r\\n\\r\\nThere are 19 one-sentence and 16 two-sentence paragraphs in this subset. There are also paragraphs with seven, eight, and nine approximate sentences. This directly argues against making “three to five sentences per paragraph” a universal rule. The noticeable feature is variation matched to purpose, with space around a new task or example.\\r\\n\\r\\nRead the draft aloud. Listen for three failures: several dense ideas in one breath; a string of clipped statements that never connect; a recurring catchphrase that sounds inserted. Fix the reasoning and breath before counting words.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Contractions are normal; expansion creates contrast\\r\\n\\r\\nThe source uses contractions throughout: I\'m, you\'re, we\'ve, we\'ll, there\'s, doesn\'t, don\'t, can\'t, couldn\'t, isn\'t, and what\'s. This includes serious explanation and procedure, not only playful asides.\\r\\n\\r\\nIt sometimes expands a form for emphasis. “If I **am** breathing” makes the presence of the sufficient condition audible. We can use the same mechanism with new language:\\r\\n\\r\\n> You don\'t know whether the parcel has a sticker. You **do** know it was inspected.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not mechanically contract every phrase. Keep a fuller form when it makes the distinction easier to hear.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Punctuation follows the voice\\r\\n\\r\\nUse full stops for changes in thought, colons before an example or sequence, and questions when a decision is genuinely at issue. Parentheses can hold a brief aside or notation clarification. Fragments are occasional conversational landings, not mandatory decorations.\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua\'s no-em-dash rule governs our writing. The source\'s occasional stretched spelling, all caps, ellipses, or exclamations are observations, not a punctuation recipe. Repeated “Awesome!”, “Cool,…7707 tokens truncated…lent formulations and other supplied rules still matter. State the immediate inference limits precisely. |\\r\\n| Required words are described as obligations. | Preserve modality. “Interviewees must bring ID” can assert an obligation, not prove compliance. Diagram the stated requirement unless the facts establish compliance. |\\r\\n| Indicator usually comes before target. | Read its full grammatical target. Targets can precede the indicator, and familiar words can serve other roles in context. |\\r\\n| Shorten conditions to one or two letters, never more than four. | Joshua\'s clear condensed labels govern. Keep negation, scope, qualifiers, and readability. A short label that loses meaning is not an improvement. |\\r\\n| Try a personalized sufficient guess. | Compare with the whole ordinary meaning and look for a counterexample. A feeling that an arrow is plausible is not enough. |\\r\\n| Original and contrapositive training. | Explain why a drill requires explicit work and when test-day practice may differ. Do not turn a training requirement into a universal performance rule. |\\r\\n| “Always” is in a necessary-family teaching list. | Establish the sentence\'s subject and relationship. It is not a universal instruction to place the next word on the right. |\\r\\n| Confidence guarantees the diagram is correct. | Confidence can grow from practice, but correctness rests on preserving meaning and valid reasoning. Provide checks. |\\r\\n| Timing and learning claims are absolute. | Treat them as the author\'s advice unless independently supported. Give a practical explanation without invented evidence. |\\r\\n| References to Logic Games, a book, page 148, or named source tools. | Preserve the teaching function only where our course has an actual equivalent. Do not import obsolete or unavailable context. |\\r\\n| A theme makes a drill memorable. | Keep each sentence logically interpretable and its answer reviewed. Novelty must not obscure the condition or require untaught knowledge. |\\r\\n\\r\\nFor the parcel example, three possible cases distinguish the permitted relationship from an invalid reverse:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Blue sticker and inspected: fits the rule.\\r\\n- Inspected without a blue sticker: also fits the rule.\\r\\n- Blue sticker without inspection: breaks the rule.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe rule does not itself say any such parcel exists. Examples of possible cases illustrate consistency, not existence claims. This distinction matters when moving from individual facts to general rules.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Calibration examples for different LSAT surfaces\\r\\n\\r\\nAll examples below are original drafts for this reference. They demonstrate writing mechanisms; they are not assigned work or approved curriculum.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Explain sufficient and necessary without rushing\\r\\n\\r\\n> Every parcel with a blue sticker has been inspected.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Suppose yours has a blue sticker. That\'s enough to know it has been inspected. You don\'t need another fact about the parcel. The rule has already told you what must be true of every parcel with that sticker.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We call the blue sticker the **sufficient condition**. Sufficient means enough. Here, enough to establish inspection under this rule.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Inspection is the **necessary condition**. A blue-sticker parcel has to meet that requirement. Otherwise it would be an exception to a rule that allows no exceptions.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Now suppose a parcel has been inspected. Does it have to have a blue sticker?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> We still don\'t know. Inspection was required for the blue-sticker parcels. The shop never said those were the only parcels it inspected.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis returns to meaning at every term. The example does not assert why the shop uses stickers or when they are applied. Those extra facts are unnecessary.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Teach a necessary expression through its whole meaning\\r\\n\\r\\n> Editing this newsletter requires an account.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> What does the sentence say the editor needs? An account. Keep that complete idea on the required side of the relationship:\\r\\n>\\r\\n> **Edits this newsletter → Has an account**\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Read it back: if someone edits this newsletter, they have an account. That matches the sentence.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Try the reverse. If someone has an account, do they necessarily edit the newsletter? The sentence hasn\'t told us that. An account could belong to someone who only reads it.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe final possible counterexample is introduced as something consistent with the sentence, not an asserted fact about this system. Technical placement has a semantic reason.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Give a flashcard a reasoning task\\r\\n\\r\\n**Front**\\r\\n\\r\\n> Every package in Locker 4 has been scanned. A package has been scanned. Must it be in Locker 4? Why?\\r\\n\\r\\n**Back**\\r\\n\\r\\n> No. The rule tells us about packages already in Locker 4. It doesn\'t say every scanned package goes there.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is more useful than a card that only asks “Necessary condition = which side?” Keep simple recall cards when recall is the actual skill; do not mistake that for complete reasoning practice.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Make feedback identify the missed connection\\r\\n\\r\\n> You used the sentence in the reverse direction. “Only registered visitors enter the archive” requires registration for entry. It hasn\'t said every registered visitor enters. Read the diagram as **Enters → Registered** and compare it with the sentence.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe feedback names the mistake, shows the relevant meaning, and gives a repair. It avoids generic praise, mockery, and labels such as “weak reasoning.”\\r\\n\\r\\n### Explain an ordinary learning objection\\r\\n\\r\\n> “I understood the sentence. Why write it down?”\\r\\n>\\r\\n> With one short rule, you may not need to. When a passage gives you several relationships, a diagram lets you compare them without rereading the wording each time. In this exercise, write the relationship so we can check that you kept its direction and complete ideas.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe answer gives a decision criterion and distinguishes the purpose of this exercise from a blanket rule about every test question.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Transfer the voice to another LSAT topic\\r\\n\\r\\n> A conclusion is the claim the author is asking you to accept. The other statements are supposed to support it.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Nora says, “The library should stay open later because every evening seat was taken this week.” What is she trying to persuade us of?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> That the library should stay open later. The full seats are her reason. She expects that reason to support the proposed change.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> You don\'t have to agree with her. First, separate what she wants you to accept from what she gives you in support.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe same mechanism works outside conditionals: definition, small example, question, explanation, and a useful boundary. No conditional topic has been imported into the conclusion lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Revise the draft in a useful order\\r\\n\\r\\n### First, check the reasoning and scope\\r\\n\\r\\nList what is given, what follows, and why. Try to construct a case that satisfies the given information but makes the proposed conclusion false. If that case is possible, revise the logic before polishing the voice. Check modality, negation, quantifier scope, and whether the learner has actually been taught every required operation.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor a rewrite, preserve Joshua\'s established method and explicit lesson scope. The new reference governs delivery. It does not authorize removing content that students need or adding source topics the current assignment does not cover.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Then, check the learner\'s experience\\r\\n\\r\\nRead as someone who has never seen the notation. Can they tell what the concept is? Can they answer the first question with what the page has taught? Does each new term refer to an idea they have seen? Does the page tell them why the correct answer follows?\\r\\n\\r\\nPut the explanation beside the point where it is needed. Do not rely on an interaction to imply a distinction the prose never explains. A student who cannot use the animation must still be able to learn from the text.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Then, listen to the voice\\r\\n\\r\\nRead aloud at an ordinary teaching pace. Replace stiff phrasing with the words the teacher would naturally use. Keep the intermediate thoughts. Vary sentence length where the task changes. Remove repeated catchphrases, inflated enthusiasm, branded metaphors, and irrelevant asides.\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not repair generic prose by scattering “Cool,” “Let\'s,” or “That\'s it” through it. Repair the missing reasoning, the abrupt transition, or the abstract example.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Finally, verify the student surface\\r\\n\\r\\nCheck the actual prompt, answer state, labels, buttons, diagrams, and explanations. A good note can be undermined by a shell that exposes internal planning or reveals the answer too soon. Preview desktop and mobile when the interface changes. Keep the instructor\'s planning map separate from what the learner sees.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Use this rubric before handing over LSAT writing\\r\\n\\r\\nScore each dimension from 0 to 2: **0** absent or misleading; **1** partly present but needing revision; **2** clear and usable. This is an editorial tool, not a validated learning measure. A logical error or scope violation requires revision regardless of the total.\\r\\n\\r\\n| Dimension | What a strong draft does |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| **Ordinary meaning** | Defines the idea in language the reader can understand before notation. |\\r\\n| **Concrete anchor** | Uses an original, small, unambiguous situation and states needed assumptions. |\\r\\n| **Visible reasoning** | Shows the intermediate connection instead of asserting a result. |\\r\\n| **Point of view** | Keeps the reader involved; uses teacher narration purposefully. |\\r\\n| **Cadence** | Gives complex thoughts room and short conclusions a clear place to land. |\\r\\n| **Vocabulary** | Keeps useful technical terms, explains them, and avoids internal jargon. |\\r\\n| **Questions and pauses** | Asks a genuine decision and gives an appropriate chance to answer. |\\r\\n| **Boundaries** | Shows what the information leaves open and why a tempting move fails. |\\r\\n| **Progression** | Each operation has a prerequisite, a reason to appear, and adequate practice. |\\r\\n| **Transfer** | Fresh questions require the taught skill, with reasoned feedback. |\\r\\n| **Tone and warmth** | Expects effort, supports the next action, and never mocks uncertainty. |\\r\\n| **Presentation** | Examples, comparisons, notation, and interactions clarify the reasoning. |\\r\\n\\r\\nDo not treat a high total as proof of an identical voice. Use the original source and Joshua\'s response to calibrate the subjective feel. His concrete corrections override a score.\\r\\n\\r\\n## A reusable writing brief\\r\\n\\r\\nUse this when giving another writer or agent the task. Supply the actual source, lesson scope, prerequisite knowledge, and approved method along with it.\\r\\n\\r\\n```text\\r\\nWrite this LSAT material in Joshua\'s selected teaching voice.\\r\\nRead wiki/teaching-voice.md, references/lsat-teaching-voice-standard.md,\\r\\nand wiki/COPY-CORRECTIONS.md before drafting.\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep the reader beside the teacher. Start with the ordinary meaning of\\r\\nthe idea, then make it concrete with an original, intuitive example.\\r\\nShow each small inference in natural language. Ask the question a learner\\r\\nwould actually need to answer here. When the question is practice, leave\\r\\nroom for an attempt before revealing the reasoning.\\r\\n\\r\\nVary sentence length by purpose. Let explanations breathe and use short\\r\\nsentences to settle a consequence or a limit. Use contractions naturally.\\r\\nTeach the technical term when there is a clear idea to attach it to.\\r\\nRepeat an anchor only when the repetition changes the learner\'s view.\\r\\nShow a tempting mistake and how to detect it when that distinction matters.\\r\\n\\r\\nPreserve Joshua\'s method, the exact logical strength, complete conditions,\\r\\nand the selected topic scope. Give fresh practice with explained answers.\\r\\nDo not copy the reference\'s examples, jokes, personal claims, or procedural\\r\\ncounts. No em dashes, hype, invented evidence, internal stage language,\\r\\nor decorative catchphrases. Light humor is optional and must help the lesson.\\r\\n\\r\\nRead the result aloud, check every inference, and review the student-facing\\r\\nprompt and answer states. If the reader cannot hear why the next thought\\r\\nfollows, revise the explanation before polishing the surface.\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n## Keep this reference current\\r\\n\\r\\nThis file is the detailed method reference, not a second canonical brand voice. Add to it every time a\\r\\ncorrection is made.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The rules these corrections came from\\r\\n\\r\\nThree rules already existed and all three leaked anyway, because each was\\r\\nenforced on the components that happened to exist when it was written. A surface\\r\\nadded later starts uncovered.\\r\\n\\r\\n- **No em dashes, ever.** [[teaching-voice]], Core voice.\\r\\n- **No internal vocabulary in student copy.** `projects/lsatu/src/features/activity-centre/CONTEXT.md`\\r\\n  carries the glossary and marks what to avoid.\\r\\n- **Every CSS token a stylesheet uses must be defined in it.** `projects/lsatu/CLAUDE.md`.\\r\\n\\r\\nGuards now live with the content rather than with each component:\\r\\n`content/instructions-voice.test.ts` checks the authored instructions, so every\\r\\nsurface that renders them is covered, including surfaces not written yet.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Corrections\\r\\n\\r\\n### Conditional opening: define the words before using them (2026-10-03)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua\'s marked browser paragraphs used “direction” and “guarantee” before making their meaning clear. The purpose paragraph also described an argument accepting more than its information supports without showing what that meant. Teach what a rule lets you conclude in plain language, then attach the vocabulary to a concrete relationship. Explain sufficient as enough and necessary as required before relying on those roles. Show what the must-arrow records and why English clause order does not determine the two sides.\\r\\n\\r\\n2026-10-03 clarification: explicitly distinguish the indicator from the complete condition it refers to. Sufficient goes left; necessary goes right. The indicator itself is not a condition in the diagram. Show the same relationship with if at the beginning and in the middle, and show necessary targets both before and after requirement language. Neither sentence position nor the words immediately following the indicator determine placement. Preserve if versus only if as different complete expressions.\\r\\n\\r\\nA rule describes what would follow **if** a condition were true; it does not say that condition happened. Bold that “if” and use meaningful in-view motion to expose the connection, with a static reduced-motion equivalent. Replace compressed ready-order wording with a natural full sentence. Give each paragraph and interaction a specific teaching job. These corrections supplement the canonical voice standard rather than adding a new writing register.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Generic reasoning prompts → concrete numbered demonstrations (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua marked four parts of the V6 opening: \\"Read each whole idea,\\" \\"Find what the statements guarantee,\\" the abstract first sentence about information, and the paragraph combining application and linking. They named goals without showing a useful action or explanation. Replace them with numbered, separate scenarios. Show the fact and rule that prove a conclusion about one case; separately show two matching rules and their new conditional conclusion. Labels should identify actual inputs or outputs. Review the whole note for repeated umbrella instructions and make task instructions executable. This follows the teaching voice: specific, concrete, short sentences, with air between distinct ideas.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Fact and rule definitions must explain the inference (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua rejected definitions that remained abstract and an explanation that did not clearly distinguish applying a rule from linking rules. Define the inputs with examples, then show the matching step and exact output. A case fact plus a rule proves something about that case. Two connecting rules produce another conditional rule without establishing a case exists. Adding a fact to the chain is a separate step. Explain all four fact situations and a hidden chain revealed by contraposition rather than leaving them implicit in an interactive model. Rules include general logical relationships, not only policies or obligations.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Boxed `L -> R` → bold teaching notation **L → R** (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua rejected the recap\'s small monospace arrow inside a pale code box. It looked like implementation text and weakened the explanation. Use a real, clearly weighted arrow in ordinary teaching typography. Explain its complete conditions before shortening them. The Some, Most, and All reference also governs the progression: introduce the whole idea, develop the individual components, then compare and combine them. A visual refresh must review that sequence, not only colors and boxes.\\r\\n\\r\\n### \\"Concept lesson\\" → the actual reasoning title (2026-09-30)\\r\\n\\r\\nThe recap preview exposed an internal label above the student lesson. Joshua explicitly rejected it. Use a title such as \\"Facts, Rules, and What Follows\\" and headings that teach the reasoning. Every statement in this file must be true of all of LSAT U.\\\\n\\\\nA rule that binds one surface does not belong here. It goes in that surface\'s brief under `.impeccable/surfaces/`. This split is deliberate and is the correction to a real failure: the previous PRODUCT.md was written on 2026-05-02 for the Intro to LR bootcamp alone, then widened app-wide on 2026-05-08 in a commit whose stated purpose was adding messenger principles. Bootcamp anti-references silently became binding on the drills, and stayed binding for four months. A one-surface rule written into an app-wide file has no boundary that can hold it. Keeping the file app-wide only removes the mechanism.\\\\n\\\\nThe repo already carries eight bounded contexts with their own glossaries (`CONTEXT-MAP.md`). Surface-specific product truth follows those boundaries, not this file.\\\\n\\\\n## Platform\\\\n\\\\nweb\\\\n\\\\n## Users\\\\n\\\\n**Primary: Aspiring Attorneys clients.** Students who are paying Joshua for one-to-one LSAT coaching. They have consultations, scheduled sessions, transcripts, assigned work, and a real back-and-forth with him. The platform is where their coaching lives between sessions. They arrive already knowing who their coach is, and design decisions are made for them first.\\\\n\\\\n**Secondary: independent self-study learners.** Students using the platform without an active coaching relationship. They are served by the same surfaces but are not the audience a tradeoff is resolved in favour of.\\\\n\\\\n**Operator: Joshua.** The sole instructor and the product, voice, and content authority. He assigns work, publishes material, reviews student activity, and answers messages. He works from any device at any hour, so operator surfaces are as responsive as student surfaces.\\\\n\\\\n## Product Purpose\\\\n\\\\nLSAT U is the operational platform for Joshua\'s coaching practice. It delivers the method, holds the student\'s work, and keeps the coaching relationship live between sessions.\\\\n\\\\nFor a student: one place that knows what they have done, what they got wrong, and what to do next.\\\\n\\\\nFor Joshua: one workspace to assign, publish, review, and reply without losing the one-to-one feel that his practice is sold on.\\\\n\\\\nSuccess is a student who logs in without being chased, knows the next action without asking, and can point to what improved.\\\\n\\\\n## Positioning\\\\n\\\\n**A real coach is in it.**\\\\n\\\\nThe claim a competing product cannot truthfully copy is that a named human being is on the other side of the platform, has met this student, and has looked at this student\'s work. Assignments come from him. Messages are answered by him. The material was authored by him. Nothing in the product should be built in a way that would still be true if the coach were removed, and nothing should imply a coach is present where one is not.\\\\n\\\\n## Operating Context\\\\n\\\\nThe platform sits inside a coaching practice that runs partly outside it. Future work must not assume the app is the whole system.\\\\n\\\\n- Coaching sessions happen on video and are transcribed. Session records, notes, and recaps originate outside the app.\\\\n- Booking and payment run through their own flow (packages, booking passes, a public booking microsite, single sessions).\\\\n- Students also practice on third-party platforms. Work done elsewhere is real work, and the app is not the only record of a student\'s effort.\\\\n- Joshua authors material ahead of time and assigns it, rather than the system generating it on demand.\\\\n- Students use both desktop and mobile, in focused study blocks and in short check-ins.\\\\n\\\\n## Capabilities and Constraints\\\\n\\\\nConfirmed surfaces: authentication and onboarding, the foyer, the classroom, guided drills and the question bank, full-passage Reading Comprehension, the Activity Centre, the Testing Centre and practice test runs, the wrong answer journal, saved sets, analytics and history, scheduling and booking, the inbox, the bootcamps, and an admin and teacher workspace.\\\\n\\\\nTechnical constraints:\\\\n\\\\n- React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, shadcn/ui and Radix primitives, React Router, TanStack Query, Supabase.\\\\n- One motion library (`framer-motion`). One primary icon library (`lucide-react`). New work composes existing primitives before introducing a new dependency.\\\\n- Deployment is not a side effect of pushing to `main`. Production at lsatprep.study requires an explicit publish step.\\\\n- Database migrations in `supabase/migrations/` are an archive, not an applied ledger. Production schema changes go through their own path, and UI must not assume a table exists because a migration file does.\\\\n\\\\nTerminology is not defined here. It is defined per bounded context and mapped by `CONTEXT-MAP.md`. A word can carry different weight in different contexts, and collapsing them has already caused real bugs (a **flag** is not a **wrong answer**; **Set** and **Position** were separated for this reason).\\\\n\\\\n## Brand Commitments\\\\n\\\\n- **Name:** LSAT U, operating under Aspiring Attorneys. Production domain lsatprep.study.\\\\n- **No em-dashes in anything a student or prospect reads.** Joshua does not type them. A stray em-dash reads as machine-written and costs trust. This binds computed copy, utility copy, and authored copy alike.\\\\n- **Voice: undecided, deliberately.** The previous record carried a \\\\\\"coach voice, not industry voice\\\\\\" principle and two named voice registers (R1 procedural, R2 metaphor-led). Both were removed on 2026-09-05 by Joshua\'s decision, on the grounds that they were not stated clearly enough to be usable. They are being redone. Until a replacement is written, no work should cite the old voice rules, and no work should invent a voice rule to fill the gap. Route student-facing copy to Joshua.\\\\n\\\\n## Evidence on Hand\\\\n\\\\nReal:\\\\n\\\\n- A live production deployment at lsatprep.study with real enrolled students.\\\\n- Authored LSAT curriculum: bootcamp modules, guided drill banks, RC passages with per-question explanations, and practice test content.\\\\n- Real student work in the database: attempts, sessions, flags, wrong answers, assignments.\\\\n- A real named instructor with a real coaching practice behind the product.\\\\n\\\\nAbsent, and never to be fabricated:\\\\n\\\\n- No testimonials, case studies, press coverage, score-improvement statistics, or named customer references exist in this repo. Do not write them into any surface.\\\\n- No pricing, licensing, or availability claims are established here.\\\\n- No third-party or copyright framing anywhere in student-facing copy.\\\\n\\\\n## Product Principles\\\\n\\\\n1. **Truthfulness over performance.** Every number, badge, streak, status, and progress claim traces to real stored data. An honest empty state beats invented content. If nothing has been assigned, the product says so and stops. This is the one principle carried forward unchanged from the previous record, and it is the hardest of the five.\\\\n\\\\n2. **Compute the next step; do not present a grid.** A student arriving at a surface should be told what to do, not shown a menu and left to choose. Reveal copy addresses what the student actually chose, not a generic key.\\\\n\\\\n4. **A measurement is never a gate.** Drills and checks measure after teaching. A miss is framed as the next thing to work on, not a grade or a failure. Nothing in the product rewards attendance rather than work.\\\\n\\\\n5. **The coach is not simulated.** Where the product speaks for Joshua, it is because Joshua said it. Where he has not, the product does not fill the silence with something that sounds like him. This one is a house standard above the floor, not part of it: 44x44 is WCAG 2.5.5, which is Level AAA. The binding target-size rule is 2.5.8 at 24x24, so a control that clears 24x24 on a fine pointer clears the floor and is not a defect.\\\\n- A dense row of marks that exists to be read at a glance is the one place the 44x44 house standard yields. The Report Card\'s ledger is 22 to 26 ticks inside an 820px card; at 44px wide they would need 968 to 1144px, so meeting the standard means scrolling or wrapping, and the ledger stops being a single picture of the run. They are 44 tall and 28 to 30 wide, they clear 2.5.8, and that is the settled answer rather than an open defect. Joshua\'s call, 2026-09-09.\\\\n- Where a control has to stay small because it sits in chrome set in 11 or 13px type, the 44x44 target may be an explicit transparent overlay centred on the control instead of the control\'s own box. An overlay is a target somebody designed and it is proved by hit-testing the four edges; wrapped text is an accident and still does not count. The runner\'s rail controls, the door\'s crumb out and the demonstration\'s Play button are all built this way.\\\\n- Screen readers are informed of state that changes without a page load: unread counts, send confirmations, and live updates.\\\\n- Contrast is verified against what actually renders in the browser, not against the token values a theme is assumed to apply. ── Teacher workspace (theme-independent, light ground only) ──\\\\n  teacher-accent: \\\\\\"#c7841f\\\\\\"\\\\n  teacher-accent-hover: \\\\\\"#af7318\\\\\\"\\\\n  teacher-accent-strong: \\\\\\"#895910\\\\\\"\\\\n  teacher-accent-soft: \\\\\\"#e0a648\\\\\\"\\\\ntypography:\\\\n  body:\\\\n    fontFamily: \\\\\\"Lexend, Outfit, ui-sans-serif, system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif\\\\\\"\\\\n    fontSize: \\\\\\"14px\\\\\\"\\\\n    fontWeight: 400\\\\n    lineHeight: 1.6\\\\n    fontFeature: \\\\\\"\'rlig\' 1, \'calt\' 1, \'cv11\' 1\\\\\\"\\\\n  title:\\\\n    fontFamily: \\\\\\"Lexend, Outfit, ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif\\\\\\"\\\\n    fontSize: \\\\\\"24px\\\\\\"\\\\n    fontWeight: 600\\\\n    lineHeight: 1\\\\n    letterSpacing: \\\\\\"-0.025em\\\\\\"\\\\n  label:\\\\n    fontFamily: \\\\\\"Lexend, Outfit, ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif\\\\\\"\\\\n    fontSize: \\\\\\"14px\\\\\\"\\\\n    fontWeight: 500\\\\n    lineHeight: 1.4\\\\n  question:\\\\n    fontFamily: \\\\\\"Outfit, ui-sans-serif, system-ui, -apple-system, sans-serif\\\\\\"\\\\n    fontSize: \\\\\\"16px\\\\\\"\\\\n    fontWeight: 400\\\\n    lineHeight: 1.6\\\\n  hall-display:\\\\n    fontFamily: \\\\\\"Fraunces, \'Iowan Old Style\', \'Times New Roman\', serif\\\\\\"\\\\n    fontWeight: 380\\\\n    lineHeight: 1.1\\\\n    letterSpacing: \\\\\\"-0.015em\\\\\\"\\\\n  hall-inscription:\\\\n    fontFamily: \\\\\\"Cinzel, \'Trajan Pro\', \'Times New Roman\', serif\\\\\\"\\\\n    fontWeight: 500\\\\n    letterSpacing: \\\\\\"0.05em\\\\\\"\\\\n  hall-mono:\\\\n    fontFamily: \\\\\\"\'IBM Plex Mono\', ui-monospace, \'SF Mono\', monospace\\\\\\"\\\\n    fontSize: \\\\\\"13px\\\\\\"\\\\n    fontWeight: 400\\\\n    letterSpac…1777 tokens truncated…our, the answer is type and space.\\\\n\\\\n**The Named Ground Rule.** No colour is written as a literal hex in a component. It resolves from a token, and a token that resolves to nothing is a defect, not a subtle effect. Three colour names in this codebase pointed at variables that were never defined, and the product silently lost its focus ring for five months.\\\\n\\\\n## Typography\\\\n\\\\n**Workroom Body:** Lexend (with Outfit, then the system stack)\\\\n**Hall Display:** Fraunces (with Iowan Old Style, Times New Roman, serif)\\\\n**Hall Inscription:** Cinzel (with Trajan Pro, serif)\\\\n**Mono:** IBM Plex Mono\\\\n**Question Lock:** Outfit, held deliberately for LSAT question surfaces\\\\n\\\\n**Character:** The Workroom is one humanist sans doing everything, sized and weighted rather than swapped. The Hall is a serif institution: an optical serif for its headings and an inscriptional face for its few carved lines. The split is the whole typographic idea. Inside, type gets out of the way; at the door, type is the architecture.\\\\n\\\\n### Hierarchy\\\\n\\\\n- **Title** (600, 24px, line-height 1, tracking -0.025em): card and section headings in the Workroom.\\\\n- **Body** (400, 14px rising to 16px at 640px and above, line-height 1.6): everything a student reads in the Workroom chrome.\\\\n- **Question** (400, 16px, line-height 1.6, Outfit): LSAT stimulus and answer choices. Font-locked to Outfit even though the rest of the app moved to Lexend, so question text does not shift when the shell\'s face changes.\\\\n- **Label** (500, 14px): button and control labels.\\\\n- **Hall Display** (380, fluid, tracking -0.015em, Fraunces): Hall headings. The unusually light 380 weight is the point; it reads as carved rather than printed.\\\\n- **Hall Inscription** (500, tracking 0.05em, Cinzel): the Hall\'s few short carved lines. Never body copy.\\\\n- **Hall Mono** (400, 13px, tracking 0.04em, IBM Plex Mono): the Hall\'s instrument labels.\\\\n\\\\n### Named Rules\\\\n\\\\n**The One Face Rule.** The Workroom uses a single family. Hierarchy is built from size, weight and space. A second family inside the Workroom is a defect unless it is the Outfit question lock.\\\\n\\\\n**The Question Never Moves Rule.** LSAT question text is font-locked. A change to the shell\'s typeface must not reflow a passage a student is mid-way through reading.\\\\n\\\\n**The Serif Stays At The Door Rule.** Fraunces and Cinzel belong to the Hall. A serif appearing in the Workroom chrome means the seam has leaked.\\\\n\\\\n## Layout\\\\n\\\\nThe Workroom is a centred single column with generous side gutters. The container centres by default, carries 32px of horizontal padding, and stops widening at 1400px.\\\\n\\\\nBreakpoints are the framework defaults up to 1280px, with the largest step pulled in to 1400px. Body type steps from 14px to 16px at 640px, and form controls are forced to 16px below 768px so that iOS does not zoom the page when a field takes focus. Named breakpoints `phone` (up to 600px), `tablet` (601 to 900px) and `desktop` (901px and up) exist for bootcamp surfaces.\\\\n\\\\nSpacing runs on a 4px base. The steps in real use are 4, 8, 16, 24 and 32. Card padding is 24px on all sides; button padding is 8px vertical and 16px horizontal.\\\\n\\\\nReading measure matters more here than in most products. Passage and stimulus text is held to a comfortable line length rather than allowed to run the full container width.\\\\n\\\\n### Named Rules\\\\n\\\\n**The Reading Measure Rule.** Any surface carrying an LSAT passage, stimulus, or explanation constrains its own line length. The container\'s maximum is a ceiling for layout, never a licence for prose.\\\\n\\\\n## Elevation & Depth\\\\n\\\\n**Flat, with hairline separation.** Surfaces sit on the page rather than above it. A card is distinguished from its ground by a one-pixel border and, where more is needed, by one step of background tone. There are no drop shadows in the Workroom.\\\\n\\\\nThis is a decision, not a description. The codebase currently ships five shadow tokens tuned for a dark ground, from `0 1px 3px rgba(0,0,0,0.4)` up to `0 8px 32px rgba(0,0,0,0.7)`, and applies the smallest of them to every card. Because the app ships light by default, those shadows land at 40 percent black under a white card. The light theme never redefined them, and the one glow token is white, so it is invisible on white. The tokens are retired by this record and the code has not caught up yet.\\\\n\\\\nThe Hall is the exception and keeps its own depth: fixed ambience gradients, a grain overlay, and an inset highlight on its call to action. That depth is atmospheric rather than structural, and it does not transfer.\\\\n\\\\n### Named Rules\\\\n\\\\n**The Flat Rule.** Depth in the Workroom comes from a hairline or a tonal step. A `box-shadow` on a Workroom surface is a defect.\\\\n\\\\n**The Two-Step Rule.** Page, then card, then at most one raised step. A surface that needs a fourth level of layering is a surface that needs restructuring.\\\\n\\\\n## Shapes\\\\n\\\\nCorners are gently rounded and consistent: 8px for cards and containers, 6px for buttons and inputs, 4px for the smallest chips and insets, and a full pill only for genuine badges. The scale derives from one 0.5rem radius token, so a change to the base moves the whole system together.\\\\n\\\\nThe Hall uses a near-square 2px radius instead. Its edges are cut, not softened, which is what separates a carved surface from a card.\\\\n\\\\nBorders are one pixel. There is no second border weight in the Workroom.\\\\n\\\\n### Named Rules\\\\n\\\\n**The Hairline Rule.** One pixel, always. A thicker border used as a coloured accent stripe on the leading edge of a surface is banned, including when faked with an inset shadow. Active state is carried by background tone.\\\\n\\\\n## Components\\\\n\\\\n### Buttons\\\\n\\\\n- **Character:** precise and quiet. A button is a plain rectangle with a label. It darkens slightly on hover and does nothing else. It does not lift, does not cast a shadow, and does not scale on press.\\\\n- **Shape:** gently rounded (6px).\\\\n- **Primary:** ink fill (`#121212`), page-coloured label, 8px by 16px padding.\\\\n- **Outline:** page background, one-pixel field border, ink label.\\\\n- **Ghost:** no fill at rest, a tonal fill on hover.\\\\n- **Sizes:** default 44px tall, small 40px, large 48px, icon 44 by 44. Every size clears the 44px touch minimum by being that height, never by relying on wrapped text or padding accidents.\\\\n- **Focus:** a solid two-pixel ink outline, offset two pixels from the edge. This is the only focus treatment in the Workroom.\\\\n- **Hall CTA:** 60px tall, near-square corners, transparent fill over a bronze hairline, with a bronze sheen that sweeps across on hover and a cyan outline on focus.\\\\n\\\\n### Cards / Containers\\\\n\\\\n- **Corner:** 8px.\\\\n- **Background:** card white on the page ground.\\\\n- **Border:** one-pixel hairline. This is what separates the card, not a shadow.\\\\n- **Shadow:** none.\\\\n- **Padding:** 24px, with header, content and footer sharing that inset.\\\\n\\\\n### Inputs / Fields\\\\n\\\\n- **Style:** page background, one-pixel field border, 6px corners, 44px minimum height, 8px by 12px padding.\\\\n- **Focus:** the same two-pixel ink outline as buttons, offset two pixels. Do not express focus as a border colour change alone; a border shift is too quiet to serve as the only indicator.\\\\n- **Mobile:** 16px text below 768px, so focusing a field never zooms the viewport.\\\\n\\\\n### Navigation\\\\n\\\\nNeutral chrome throughout. The sidebar runs one tonal step off the page ground with a hairline edge, and the active item is marked by background tone rather than by a coloured rule on its leading edge.\\\\n\\\\n### Signature Component: the scoped world\\\\n\\\\nThe product\'s distinctive pattern is not a control, it is a container. A room commits fully to its own palette, typefaces and atmosphere behind a single wrapper class, and nothing inside it leaks out. Scene layers are `aria-hidden` furniture painted beneath the content, so the accessible tree is identical whether the room is painted or bare. A new world is added by writing a new wrapper and its prefixed tokens, never by adding hex to a shared component.\\\\n\\\\n## Do\'s and Don\'ts\\\\n\\\\n### Do:\\\\n\\\\n- **Do** resolve every colour from a token, and treat a token that resolves to nothing as a defect. Verify a new token renders before documenting it.\\\\n- **Do** give every interactive element a visible focus indicator: a solid two-pixel ink outline offset two pixels in the Workroom, cyan in the Hall.\\\\n- **Do** check contrast against the ground the colour will actually land on, in the theme that actually ships, in a browser. The theme file has read as correct while the page rendered a light card on a near-black ground.\\\\n- **Do** separate surfaces with a one-pixel hairline and one tonal step.\\\\n- **Do** keep colour semantic: correct, incorrect, warning, danger. Nothing else earns it.\\\\n- **Do** scope a new room\'s identity behind its own wrapper class with prefixed tokens, the way the bootcamps and the eight Activity worlds already do.\\\\n- **Do** hold LSAT passage and stimulus text to a readable line length, and leave it on the Outfit question lock.\\\\n- **Do** end every world\'s stylesheet with a `prefers-reduced-motion` block that stops continuous motion rather than speeding it up.\\\\n\\\\n### Don\'t:\\\\n\\\\n- **Don\'t** add a `box-shadow` to a Workroom surface. Depth is hairline and tone.\\\\n- **Don\'t** carry a Hall colour into the Workroom. Bronze reads 8.58:1 on the Hall\'s night and 2.30:1 on the Workroom\'s page.\\\\n- **Don\'t** introduce a warm or metallic accent into the Workroom to make it feel premium. Premium here is depth, hierarchy and type.\\\\n- **Don\'t** remove the browser\'s focus outline without shipping a replacement in the same rule. `outline-none` with no working ring is worse than leaving the default alone.\\\\n- **Don\'t** animate the focus indicator. A `transition-all` on a control means the ring fades in, which delays the one signal a keyboard user depends on.\\\\n- **Don\'t** use a border thicker than one pixel as a coloured accent stripe, including when faked with an inset shadow.\\\\n- **Don\'t** put a second typeface into the Workroom chrome, and don\'t let a serif cross in from the Hall.\\\\n- **Don\'t** animate layout properties. Animate `opacity`, `transform` and `color`. No bounce, no elastic, no lift on hover.\\\\n- **Don\'t** write a hex value into a component. If a room needs its own colour, promote it to named tokens behind that room\'s wrapper.\\\\n\\\\n<!--\\\\nKnown gaps between this record and the code, as of 2026-09-05. Both now use `outline-2 outline-offset-2 outline-foreground`,\\\\n   and `transition-all` was narrowed so the ring no longer fades in. FIXED 2026-09-05. `--accent-bronze`, `--accent-warm` and `--glow-bronze` were\\\\n   consumed by tailwind.config.ts and defined in no commit in the repo\'s history.\\\\n   They arrived 2026-04-06 in \\\\\\"Imported LSATATTORNEYS project files\\\\\\". `#b06a3e` was\\\\n   inferred from a literal rgba in the `glow-sm` shadow on 2026-06-26 and written into\\\\n   the previous DESIGN.md as a brand accent it never was. The record above chooses quiet and flat.\\\\n-->\\\\n\\",\\n  \\"designPath\\": \\"DESIGN.md\\",\\n  \\"migrated\\": false,\\n  \\"contextDir\\": \\"C:\\\\\\\\Users\\\\\\\\Joshu\\\\\\\\dev\\\\\\\\ai-os-projects\\\\\\\\lsatu-conditional-bootcamp\\"\\n}\\n"}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"c09ff4","wall_time_seconds":0.6006482,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":1900,"output":"Run systematic **technical** quality checks and generate a comprehensive report. Don\'t fix issues — document them for other commands to address.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is a code-level audit, not a design critique. Check what\'s measurable and verifiable in the implementation.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Diagnostic Scan\\r\\n\\r\\nRun comprehensive checks across 5 dimensions. Score each dimension 0-4 using the criteria below.\\r\\n\\r\\n### 1. Accessibility (A11y)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Check for**:\\r\\n- **Contrast issues**: Text contrast ratios < 4.5:1 (or 7:1 for AAA)\\r\\n- **Missing ARIA**: Interactive elements without proper roles, labels, or states\\r\\n- **Keyboard navigation**: Missing focus indicators, illogical tab order, keyboard traps\\r\\n- **Semantic HTML**: Improper heading hierarchy, missing landmarks, divs instead of buttons\\r\\n- **Alt text**: Missing or poor image descriptions\\r\\n- **Form issues**: Inputs without labels, poor error messaging, missing required indicators\\r\\n\\r\\n**Score 0-4**: 0=Inaccessible (fails WCAG A), 1=Major gaps (few ARIA labels, no keyboard nav), 2=Partial (some a11y effort, significant gaps), 3=Good (WCAG AA mostly met, minor gaps), 4=Excellent (WCAG AA fully met, approaches AAA)\\r\\n\\r\\n### 2. Performance\\r\\n\\r\\n**Check for**:\\r\\n- **Layout thrashing**: Reading/writing layout properties in loops\\r\\n- **Expensive animations**: Casual layout-property animation, unbounded blur/filter/shadow effects, or effects that visibly drop frames\\r\\n- **Missing optimization**: Images without lazy loading, unoptimized assets, missing will-change\\r\\n- **Bundle size**: Unnecessary imports, unused dependencies\\r\\n- **Render performance**: Unnecessary re-renders, missing memoization\\r\\n\\r\\n**Score 0-4**: 0=Severe issues (layout thrash, unoptimized everything), 1=Major problems (no lazy loading, expensive animations), 2=Partial (some optimization, gaps remain), 3=Good (mostly optimized, minor improvements possible), 4=Excellent (fast, lean, well-optimized)\\r\\n\\r\\n### 3. Theming\\r\\n\\r\\n**Check for**:\\r\\n- **Hard-coded colors**: Colors not using design tokens\\r\\n- **Broken dark mode**: Missing dark mode variants, poor contrast in dark theme\\r\\n- **Inconsistent tokens**: Using wrong tokens, mixing token types\\r\\n- **Theme switching issues**: Values that don\'t update on theme change\\r\\n\\r\\n**Score 0-4**: 0=No theming (hard-coded everything), 1=Minimal tokens (mostly hard-coded), 2=Partial (tokens exist but inconsistently used), 3=Good (tokens used, minor hard-coded values), 4=Excellent (full token system, dark mode works perfectly)\\r\\n\\r\\n### 4. Responsive Design\\r\\n\\r\\n**Check for**:\\r\\n- **Fixed widths**: Hard-coded widths that break on mobile\\r\\n- **Touch targets**: Interactive elements < 44x44px\\r\\n- **Horizontal scroll**: Content overflow on narrow viewports\\r\\n- **Text scaling**: Layouts that break when text size increases\\r\\n- **Missing breakpoints**: No mobile/tablet variants\\r\\n\\r\\n**Score 0-4**: 0=Desktop-only (breaks on mobile), 1=Major issues (some breakpoints, many failures), 2=Partial (works on mobile, rough edges), 3=Good (responsive, minor touch target or overflow issues), 4=Excellent (fluid, all viewports, proper touch targets)\\r\\n\\r\\n### 5. Anti-Patterns (CRITICAL)\\r\\n\\r\\nCheck against ALL the **DON\'T** guidelines from the parent impeccable skill (already loaded in this context). Look for AI slop tells (AI color palette, gradient text, glassmorphism, hero metrics, card grids, generic fonts) and general design anti-patterns (gray on color, nested cards, bounce easing, redundant copy).\\r\\n\\r\\n**Score 0-4**: 0=AI slop gallery (5+ tells), 1=Heavy AI aesthetic (3-4 tells), 2=Some tells (1-2 noticeable), 3=Mostly clean (subtle issues only), 4=No AI tells (distinctive, intentional design)\\r\\n\\r\\n## Generate Report\\r\\n\\r\\n### Audit Health Score\\r\\n\\r\\n| # | Dimension | Score | Key Finding |\\r\\n|---|-----------|-------|-------------|\\r\\n| 1 | Accessibility | ? | [most critical a11y issue or \\"--\\"] |\\r\\n| 2 | Performance | ? | |\\r\\n| 3 | Responsive Design | ? | |\\r\\n| 4 | Theming | ? | |\\r\\n| 5 | Anti-Patterns | ? | |\\r\\n| **Total** | | **??/20** | **[Rating band]** |\\r\\n\\r\\n**Rating bands**: 18-20 Excellent (minor polish), 14-17 Good (address weak dimensions), 10-13 Acceptable (significant work needed), 6-9 Poor (major overhaul), 0-5 Critical (fundamental issues)\\r\\n\\r\\n### Anti-Patterns Verdict\\r\\n**Start here.** Pass/fail: Does this look AI-generated? List specific tells. Be brutally honest.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Executive Summary\\r\\n- Audit Health Score: **??/20** ([rating band])\\r\\n- Total issues found (count by severity: P0/P1/P2/P3)\\r\\n- Top 3-5 critical issues\\r\\n- Recommended next steps\\r\\n\\r\\n### Detailed Findings by Severity\\r\\n\\r\\nTag every issue with **P0-P3 severity**:\\r\\n- **P0 Blocking**: Prevents task completion — fix immediately\\r\\n- **P1 Major**: Significant difficulty or WCAG AA violation — fix before release\\r\\n- **P2 Minor**: Annoyance, workaround exists — fix in next pass\\r\\n- **P3 Polish**: Nice-to-fix, no real user impact — fix if time permits\\r\\n\\r\\nFor each issue, document:\\r\\n- **[P?] Issue name**\\r\\n- **Location**: Component, file, line\\r\\n- **Category**: Accessibility / Performance / Theming / Responsive / Anti-Pattern\\r\\n- **Impact**: How it affects users\\r\\n- **WCAG/Standard**: Which standard it violates (if applicable)\\r\\n- **Recommendation**: How to fix it\\r\\n- **Suggested command**: Which command to use (prefer: $impeccable adapt, $impeccable animate, $impeccable audit, $impeccable bolder, $impeccable clarify, $impeccable colorize, $impeccable critique, $impeccable delight, $impeccable distill, $impeccable document, $impeccable harden, $impeccable layout, $impeccable onboard, $impeccable optimize, $impeccable overdrive, $impeccable polish, $impeccable quieter, $impeccable shape, $impeccable typeset)\\r\\n\\r\\n### Patterns & Systemic Issues\\r\\n\\r\\nIdentify recurring problems that indicate systemic gaps rather than one-off mistakes:\\r\\n- \\"Hard-coded colors appear in 15+ components, should use design tokens\\"\\r\\n- \\"Touch targets consistently too small (<44px) throughout mobile experience\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### Positive Findings\\r\\n\\r\\nNote what\'s working well — good practices to maintain and replicate.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Recommended Actions\\r\\n\\r\\nList recommended commands in priority order (P0 first, then P1, then P2):\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **[P?] `$command-name`** — Brief description (specific context from audit findings)\\r\\n2. **[P?] `$command-name`** — Brief description (specific context)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Rules**: Only recommend commands from: $impeccable adapt, $impeccable animate, $impeccable audit, $impeccable bolder, $impeccable clarify, $impeccable colorize, $impeccable critique, $impeccable delight, $impeccable distill, $impeccable document, $impeccable harden, $impeccable layout, $impeccable onboard, $impeccable optimize, $impeccable overdrive, $impeccable polish, $impeccable quieter, $impeccable shape, $impeccable typeset. Map findings to the most appropriate command. End with `$impeccable polish` as the final step if any fixes were recommended.\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter presenting the summary, tell the user:\\r\\n\\r\\n> You can ask me to run these one at a time, all at once, or in any order you prefer.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Re-run `$impeccable audit` after fixes to see your score improve.\\r\\n\\r\\n**IMPORTANT**: Be thorough but actionable. Too many P3 issues creates noise. Focus on what actually matters.\\r\\n\\r\\n**NEVER**:\\r\\n- Report issues without explaining impact (why does this matter?)\\r\\n- Provide generic recommendations (be specific and actionable)\\r\\n- Skip positive findings (celebrate what works)\\r\\n- Forget to prioritize (everything can\'t be P0)\\r\\n- Report false positives without verification\\r\\n\\r\\nRemember: You\'re a technical quality auditor. Document systematically, prioritize ruthlessly, cite specific code locations, and provide clear paths to improvement.\\r\\n"}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"e386d4","wall_time_seconds":0.3838318,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":1056,"output":"# Product register\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen design SERVES the product: app UIs, admin dashboards, settings panels, data tables, tools, authenticated surfaces, anything where the user is in a task.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The product slop test\\r\\n\\r\\nNot \\"would someone say AI made this\\" — familiarity is often a feature here. The test is: would a user fluent in the category\'s best tools (Linear, Figma, Notion, Raycast, Stripe come to mind) sit down and trust this interface, or pause at every subtly-off component?\\r\\n\\r\\nProduct UI\'s failure mode isn\'t flatness, it\'s strangeness without purpose: over-decorated buttons, mismatched form controls, gratuitous motion, display fonts where labels should be, invented affordances for standard tasks. The bar is earned familiarity. The tool should disappear into the task.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Typography\\r\\n\\r\\n- **System fonts are legitimate.** `-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, \\"Segoe UI\\", system-ui, sans-serif` gives you native feel on every platform. Inter is the common cross-platform default for a reason.\\r\\n- **One family is often right.** Product UIs don\'t need display/body pairing. A well-tuned sans carries headings, buttons, labels, body, data.\\r\\n- **Fixed rem scale, not fluid.** Clamp-sized headings don\'t serve product UI. Users view at consistent DPI, and a fluid h1 that shrinks in a sidebar looks worse, not better.\\r\\n- **Tighter scale ratio.** 1.125–1.2 between steps is typical. More type elements here than on brand surfaces; exaggerated contrast creates noise.\\r\\n- **Line length still applies for prose** (65–75ch). Data and compact UI can run denser — tables at 120ch+ are fine.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Color\\r\\n\\r\\nProduct defaults to Restrained. A single surface can earn Committed — a dashboard where one category color carries a report, an onboarding flow with a drenched welcome screen — but Restrained is the floor.\\r\\n\\r\\n- State-rich semantic vocabulary: hover, focus, active, disabled, selected, loading, error, warning, success, info. Standardize these.\\r\\n- Accent color used for primary actions, current selection, and state indicators only — not decoration.\\r\\n- A second neutral layer for sidebars, toolbars, and panels (slightly cooler or warmer than the content surface).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Layout\\r\\n\\r\\n- Predictable grids. Consistency IS an affordance — users navigate faster when the structure is expected.\\r\\n- Familiar patterns are features. Standard navigation (top bar, side nav), breadcrumbs, tabs, and form layouts have established user expectations. Don\'t reinvent for flavor.\\r\\n- Responsive behavior is structural (collapse sidebar, responsive table, breakpoint-driven columns), not fluid typography.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Components\\r\\n\\r\\nEvery interactive component has: default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error. Don\'t ship with half of these.\\r\\n\\r\\n- Skeleton states for loading, not spinners in the middle of content.\\r\\n- Empty states that teach the interface, not \\"nothing here.\\"\\r\\n- Consistent affordances across the surface. Same button shape. Same form-control vocabulary. Same icon style.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Motion\\r\\n\\r\\n- 150–250 ms on most transitions. Users are in flow — don\'t make them wait for choreography.\\r\\n- Motion conveys state, not decoration. State change, feedback, loading, reveal — nothing else.\\r\\n- No orchestrated page-load sequences. Product loads into a task; users don\'t want to watch it load.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Product bans (on top of the shared absolute bans)\\r\\n\\r\\n- Decorative motion that doesn\'t convey state.\\r\\n- Inconsistent component vocabulary across screens. If the \\"save\\" button looks different in two places, one is wrong.\\r\\n- Display fonts in UI labels, buttons, data.\\r\\n- Reinventing standard affordances for flavor (custom scrollbars, weird form controls, non-standard modals).\\r\\n- Heavy color or full-saturation accents on inactive states.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Product permissions\\r\\n\\r\\nProduct can afford things brand surfaces can\'t.\\r\\n\\r\\n- System fonts and familiar sans defaults (Inter, SF Pro, system-ui stacks).\\r\\n- Standard navigation patterns: top bar + side nav, breadcrumbs, tabs, command palettes.\\r\\n- Density. Tables with many rows, panels with many labels, dense information when users need it.\\r\\n- Consistency over surprise. The same visual vocabulary screen to screen is a virtue; delight is saved for moments, not pages.\\r\\n"}'}]

It has to be met, but meeting it might not be enough.**\\r\\n> For example, you have to be a student to be enrolled in law school. That makes being a student **necessary for law-school enrollment**.\\r\\n> But being a student doesn’t mean you’re enrolled in law school. You could be studying history instead.\\r\\n> **Being a student is required. It doesn’t establish enrollment on its own.**\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep “might not”: a condition may be both necessary and sufficient. Do not replace this with “something another condition can’t be true without.”\\r\\n\\r\\nExplicit page corrections:\\r\\n- Emphasize the complete consequent, “then you are a student,” and identify “you are a student” as the condition. Do not teach isolated “then” as a standalone necessary-condition indicator.\\r\\n- Law student / history student / not a student should be vertical case tabs. Keep keyboard navigation, visible selected state, and mobile stacking. This is a decision for this case comparison, not a mandate for every interaction.\\r\\n- Remove “Replay emphasis”; use a gentle continuous pulse for this page, with a static reduced-motion equivalent. This does not authorize constant pulsing on every page.\\r\\n- Make clear which facts are given and which follow. If a history case says not enrolled, make it explicitly given rather than inferring it from studying history.\\r\\n\\r\\nContent preservation checks for the conditional sequence:\\r\\n- Necessary examples retain only, only if, only when, only where, always, requires, must; explain their meaning in the complete sentence and preserve modality/scope. The arrow alone asserts neither condition as a fact, neither causation nor chronological order, and no reverse inference.\\r\\n- The lead “A must arrow shows what has to be true if another condition is true” was rejected as too abstract on 2026-10-11. We symbolize the conditional relationship with one simple sign:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"diagram\\">Sufficient  →  Necessary\\r\\n              ↑\\r\\n          Must Arrow</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>We use the Must Arrow to signify the Must Relationship. It is a reminder of the urgency of conditionals. Every conditional relationship can be written like this. We call it <em>diagramming the conditional</em>.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Here are your steps for diagramming a conditional relationship:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<ol>\\r\\n  <li>See a conditional indicator.</li>\\r\\n  <li>Draw a Must Arrow.</li>\\r\\n  <li>Place an abbreviation of the word or phrase targeted by the conditional indicator on the correct side of the Must Arrow.\\r\\n    <ul>\\r\\n      <li>Sufficient is on the left, before the Must Arrow.</li>\\r\\n      <li>Necessary is on the right, after the Must Arrow.</li>\\r\\n    </ul>\\r\\n  </li>\\r\\n  <li>Fill in the other side of the Must Arrow with whatever is left over in the statement.</li>\\r\\n</ol>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Let’s take diagramming conditionals for a spin together. We’ll start with our favorite statement:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p class=\\"example\\">If I’m breathing, then air is present.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>I see a sufficient indicator in front of breathing, so I’ll place a <strong>B</strong> in the sufficient condition:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"diagram\\">B →</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Now, I’ll fill in the other side of the Must Arrow with <strong>A</strong> for air, since that’s what’s left in the statement.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"diagram\\">B → A</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>There you go. Your first fully diagrammed conditional! Now let’s talk through the contrapositive. If the necessary condition is gone, we know the sufficient is gone as well. We can diagram the contrapositive as:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"diagram\\">~A → ~B</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"note\\">Check out the little squiggle (~) in front of the ~A and ~B. We’ll use the squiggle throughout this text to negate variables. Read the squiggle as a “not.”</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Check out a few more contrapositive examples:</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<table>\\r\\n  <thead><tr><th>Original Statement</th><th>Equivalent Contrapositive</th></tr></thead>\\r\\n  <tbody>\\r\\n    <tr><td>A → B</td><td>~B → ~A</td></tr>\\r\\n    <tr><td>Q → ~R</td><td>R → ~Q</td></tr>\\r\\n    <tr><td>~L → P</td><td>~P → L</td></tr>\\r\\n    <tr><td>~Y → ~X</td><td>X → Y</td></tr>\\r\\n  </tbody>\\r\\n</table>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p><strong>Once you have the original statement written down, you can flip and negate both sides to quickly jot down the contrapositive.</strong></p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p><strong>I don’t recommend diagramming the contrapositive on every conditional you encounter</strong> just for the sake of doing so, but sometimes it will be useful to write the conditional in its contrapositive form, either for clarity or to facilitate a chain. <strong>Conditionals can be written either way: as the original statement or as the contrapositive.</strong> Both statements are describing the same relationship.</p>\\r\\n\\r\\n<div class=\\"callout\\">\\r\\n  <p>Instead of writing the contrapositive out every time, you can just read the contrapositive when it’s relevant. Every conditional can be read two ways:</p>\\r\\n  <ol>\\r\\n    <li>Read it forwards from left to right.</li>\\r\\n    <li>Read it backwards from right to left, negating everything as you go (reading the contrapositive without having to write it out).</li>\\r\\n  </ol>\\r\\n</div>\\r\\n\\r\\n<p>Awesome! ## assistant

Both sources agree on **Sufficient → Necessary**, but they contribute different teaching pieces:

- The video makes the meaning clear: **if the left side is true, the right side must be true**. It also reads the relationship as **the left requires the right**.
- The HTML explains why we use a diagram, then builds one step by step: identify the indicator, place its condition on the correct side, and fill in the other condition.

That suggests the page should teach both the arrow’s meaning and how to construct it. Neither source supports saying the left side itself is guaranteed by the rule.

## My request:
- **The Basic Reading:** Read an arrow `A → B` as \*\*"If A is true, then B must be true"\*\*[1].
- **The "Requires" Definition:** The arrow expresses a requirement relationship—specifically, **"The left side requires the right side"** (`Left requires Right`)                            **Left Side (Sufficient Condition / Trigger):** The idea attached to the left side acts as the trigger[1]. When the left-side condition is met, the rule is activated, and the outcome on the right side necessarily follows[1].
- **Right Side (Necessary Condition / Outcome):** The idea on the right side is the required outcome whenever the trigger occurs                                                                           **What the Arrow Does NOT Do**
  - **No Backward Movement (Illegal Reversal):** Knowing that the right-side outcome occurred does not allow you to conclude that the left-side trigger happened[6]. Attempting to move backward against the direction of the arrow is an "illegal reversal"[6][7].
  - **No Power when Trigger Fails (Illegal Negation):** If you learn that the left-side trigger did not happen, the rule simply **disappears**[4]. It exerts no control over the scenario, and no conclusions can be drawn about the right side


## assistant

This gives us a clearer structure: **how to read the arrow → what each side means → what you cannot conclude.**

I’d correct one point: **the rule does not disappear when the trigger is absent.** It still holds; that fact alone tells us nothing about the right side.

The simplified teaching copy:

**Read the arrow from left to right.**

**A → B** means: **If A is true, then B must be true.**  
Another way to read it: **A requires B.**

- **Left side: sufficient condition, or trigger.** If this is true, the right side must be true.
- **Right side: necessary condition.** This is what the left side requires.

**Two conclusions the arrow does not support:**

- **B is true, so A must be true.** That reverses the relationship.
- **A is false, so B must be false.** B could still be true for another reason.

With our example: being a student does not prove law-school enrollment, and not being enrolled in law school does not prove someone is not a student.

# AGENTS.md instructions for C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os

<INSTRUCTIONS>
These AGENTS.md instructions replace all previously provided AGENTS.md instructions.

# Global rules — Joshua

These apply on **every** project on this machine, in every session. Project-level
`AGENTS.md` files add to this; they do not replace it.

Keep this file short. It reloads on every message.

---

## Who

Joshua Fisseha — `contact@aspiringattorneys.com`. Builds **LSAT U** (lsatprep.study) and
the Aspiring Attorneys brand. Teaches the LSAT: ~25 one-to-one sessions a week plus
consultations. Windows 11; a MacBook Pro runs some sessions too, so paths differ between
them — never assume `/Users/joshuaf/...` resolves here.

## Where things live

- **AI OS / second brain:** `C:\Users\Joshu\dev\ai-os` — the Obsidian vault. `context/`,
  `wiki/`, `students/`, `corpus/`, `decisions/`, `brainstorms/`, `skills/`, `projects/`.
  Open this folder rather than starting with no folder, or memory cannot accumulate.
- **Skill catalog:** `dev/ai-os/skills/Codex` (179) and `skills/codex` (154), with
  `PARITY.md` declaring deliberate single-runtime skills and `INDEX.md` cataloging them.
- **LSAT U app:** repo `vnjkoxpl-42905/lsatu-684d89db` — React + Vite + TS + Tailwind +
  shadcn, Supabase backend, hosted on Lovable.
- **GitHub:** account `vnjkoxpl-42905` (auto-generated name, correct account).

## How to work with him

- **Do the whole task.** Deliver the finished thing, then say plainly what you skipped
  and why. Don't hand back a plan when the work was asked for.
- **Look before asking.** If the answer is on disk or reachable through a connected tool,
  go get it. He has Firecrawl, Google Workspace (`gws`), and `gh` — use them.
- **Say what's actually true.** Distinguish verified from assumed, every time. If a step
  failed or was skipped, lead with that. A confident wrong answer costs more than "I
  don't know yet."
- **Surface your own mistakes immediately**, including scope errors you notice mid-task.
- Absolute dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`), never "yesterday" or "last week".
- Don't re-ask what he already answered. Don't pad with options he didn't request.

- **Dictation fixes.** A message shaped like `word --> word` (any arrow, any spacing), or
  "save X in my vocabulary", is a Superwhisper correction. Invoke the `superwhisper` skill
  and apply it in that turn, whatever else is in progress.

## Writing as Joshua

Anything published under his name — course copy, lessons, emails, posts.

Plain, direct, confident. Short sentences. Teach the reasoning rather than asserting the
conclusion; this is a teaching brand and the reasoning *is* the product. Concrete beats
abstract. Never condescend to the reader.

**Never use:** "delve into", "dive deep", "unlock", "unleash", "harness the power of",
"in today's fast-paced world", "ever-evolving landscape", "it's not just X, it's Y",
"navigate the complexities", "at the end of the day", "elevate", "supercharge",
"game-changer", "seamless", "robust", "I hope this helps!", "Great question!",
"Certainly!". No em-dash pile-ups. No paragraph opening with "Moreover," /
"Furthermore," / "Additionally,". No emoji in professional writing unless asked.

Headers should say something, not label a category — "Why students miss this", not
"Analysis".

## Safety

- **Draft by default; send only when he says "send".** Email, messages, posts are drafted
  and shown to him. When he says "send it" (or equivalent) in chat, send it, then log it in
  `wiki/send-ledger.md`. Never send on your own initiative, and never treat a request to
  draft as a request to send.
- **Never delete** files, emails, or records without explicit confirmation.
- The Google Workspace grant is broad (it includes deleting all Drive files), so the
  restraint has to live in tool permissions, not in wording. A prompt is not a permission
  layer.
- Secrets stay in `.env` and the OS keyring. Never paste a key into a note, a commit, or
  a chat.

## Tools already connected

- **Firecrawl** — CLI + 28 skills. Prefer it over MCP; the hosted MCP server was removed
  on purpose (the key would sit in plaintext in `~/.Codex.json`).
- **Google Workspace** — `gws` CLI, GCP project `ai-os-joshua`. Gmail, Calendar, Drive,
  Docs, Sheets, Slides, Tasks, People.
- **GitHub** — `gh` CLI, authenticated.

## Cost discipline

`AGENTS.md` reloads on every message, so keep this file lean. Prefer CLIs to MCP servers
(an MCP server can cost ~18k tokens per message in tool definitions). `/clear` between
unrelated tasks. Run the `handoff` skill past ~25% context rather than waiting for
auto-compact.

point of the file.*
